Lessons.Title: Intersection Points
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Solve intersections of a line and a circle or parabola as a linear–quadratic system, recognizing zero, one or two real points.
Replace y with the line expression in quadratic curve equation Solve resulting polynomial and substitute back
For ax²+bx+c=0, Δ=b²−4ac controls real root count Check curve and line at candidate

Original student task: Draw line/conic plots and show algebraic intersection correspondence; teacher assesses proof. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise hypotheses and diagrams, valid operations, independently checked results and clear explanation. Never equate a numeric answer with grading proof work.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 13, CC BY 4.0. Independently authored examples; no source artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Substitution
KeyConcepts.Definition: Replace y with the line expression in quadratic curve equation
KeyConcepts.Rule: Solve resulting polynomial and substitute back

KeyConcepts.Title: Discriminant
KeyConcepts.Definition: For ax²+bx+c=0, Δ=b²−4ac controls real root count
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two, one or zero roots for Δ>0,=0,<0

KeyConcepts.Title: Tangent intersection
KeyConcepts.Definition: A single repeated real root means tangency in suitable line–conic setting
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check curve and line at candidate

WorkedExamples.Title: Intersection Points — worked example 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Intersect line y=x and parabola y=x².
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

WorkedExamples.Title: Intersection Points — worked example 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Intersect y=1 and circle x²+y²=1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

WorkedExamples.Title: Intersection Points — worked example 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Intersect line y=3 with circle x²+y²=4.
Steps: Then x²=−5 has no real solution
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting complex roots as real plane intersections
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cartesian geometric points require real coordinates

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Solving for x without restoring y
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An intersection is an ordered pair
CommonMistakes.Correction: Substitute every root into the line

SummaryPoints: Solve intersections of a line and a circle or parabola as a linear–quadratic system, recognizing zero, one or two real points.
Two, one or zero roots for Δ>0,=0,<0
Teacher evaluation is required for original coordinate proofs and graphical submissions.

Lessons.Title: Coordinate Proof
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Use coordinates, squared distance, slope and midpoint to prove a geometric statement without relying on diagram appearance.
Midpoint of A(x1,y1),B(x2,y2) is ((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2) Opposite midpoint matches establish diagonal bisection
Equal squared lengths show congruent sides without square roots For AB=(2,3) and CD=(4,6), parallel

Original student task: Select coordinate origin and prove one quadrilateral classification; teacher reviews written logic. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise hypotheses and diagrams, valid operations, independently checked results and clear explanation. Never equate a numeric answer with grading proof work.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 14, CC BY 4.0. Independently authored examples; no source artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Midpoint
KeyConcepts.Rule: Opposite midpoint matches establish diagonal bisection

KeyConcepts.Title: Distance proof
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal squared lengths show congruent sides without square roots

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel proof
KeyConcepts.Definition: Vectors proportional ⇒ directions parallel for distinct lines

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating plotted slopes as exact proof
Comparing distance components instead of squared sums

SummaryPoints: Use coordinates, squared distance, slope and midpoint to prove a geometric statement without relying on diagram appearance.

Lessons.Title: Weighted Averages
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Partition a segment at a stated positive ratio using weighted coordinate averages, and interpret internal versus external division.
Point P at fraction t∈[0,1] from A to B is A+t(B−A) Compute each coordinate separately
If AP:PB=m:n with m,n>0 then t=m/(m+n) Distinguish segment from entire line

Original student task: Draw line and mark partition ratios in two different coordinate settings; teacher checks exact construction. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise hypotheses and diagrams, valid operations, independently checked results and clear explanation. Never equate a numeric answer with grading proof work.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 15, CC BY 4.0. Independently authored examples; no source artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Internal partition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Point P at fraction t∈[0,1] from A to B is A+t(B−A)

KeyConcepts.Title: Ratio convention
KeyConcepts.Definition: If AP:PB=m:n with m,n>0 then t=m/(m+n)

KeyConcepts.Title: External case
KeyConcepts.Definition: t outside [0,1] lies on extended line beyond segment

Lessons.Title: Weighted Averages in a Triangle
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove that all three medians concur at the centroid and compute the centroid as the average of vertex coordinates.
Segment from vertex to opposite-side midpoint Find side midpoint first
G=(A+B+C)/3 coordinatewise G=A+(2/3)(M−A)

Original student task: Construct all three medians on grid and prove their common centroid algebraically; teacher assesses diagram/proof. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise hypotheses and diagrams, valid operations, independently checked results and clear explanation. Never equate a numeric answer with grading proof work.

Lessons.Title: Lines in Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Use coordinate slopes and perpendicularity to determine and verify concurrency of triangle altitudes at the orthocenter, distinguishing special right and obtuse cases.
Line through vertex perpendicular to opposite side Find slope or use dot product
Common intersection of triangle's three altitude lines Extend altitude lines, not just segments

Original student task: Plot acute, right and obtuse triangles and verify altitude concurrency with independent slope tests; teacher scores proofs. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise hypotheses and diagrams, valid operations, independently checked results and clear explanation. Never equate a numeric answer with grading proof work.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 6 Lesson 17, CC BY 4.0. Independently authored examples; no source artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Altitude
KeyConcepts.Definition: Line through vertex perpendicular to opposite side
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find slope or use dot product
KeyConcepts.Example: For horizontal BC, altitude from A is vertical

KeyConcepts.Title: Orthocenter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Common intersection of triangle's three altitude lines
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two altitudes determine candidate; verify third
KeyConcepts.Example: For right triangle orthocenter is right-angle vertex

KeyConcepts.Title: Obtuse case
KeyConcepts.Rule: Extend altitude lines, not just segments
KeyConcepts.Example: Angle at A obtuse can place H outside

WorkedExamples.Title: Lines in Triangles — worked example 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle A=(0,0),B=(4,0),C=(0,3). Find orthocenter.
Steps: AB horizontal, altitude from C vertical x=0
AC vertical, altitude from B horizontal y=0
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

WorkedExamples.Title: Lines in Triangles — worked example 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle A=(0,2),B=(−2,0),C=(2,0). Find orthocenter.
Steps: AC has slope −1/2 so B altitude slope 2
Through B(−2,0): y=2(x+2); at x=0 y=4
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

WorkedExamples.Title: Lines in Triangles — worked example 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Verify third altitude of same triangle passes through H=(0,4).
Steps: At x=0 this yields y=2, not 4
WorkedExamples.Answer: The proposed H=(0,4) is incorrect; recheck the other altitude equations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify the candidate against original coordinate conditions and exceptional cases.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using side slope instead of negative reciprocal
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Altitude must be perpendicular to opposite side

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Declaring concurrence after only two lines without checking third
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A mistaken slope can produce false intersection

SummaryPoints: Use coordinate slopes and perpendicularity to determine and verify concurrency of triangle altitudes at the orthocenter, distinguishing special right and obtuse cases.
Two altitudes determine candidate; verify third
Teacher evaluation is required for original coordinate proofs and graphical submissions.
